title: The hymn that quotes its doubters
hook: "where is he?" some ask. "he is not," some say. a hymn to Indra quotes its doubters out loud
carry: shraddha: trust you place, even beside doubt

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agni the fire, at the wedding: witness to the vow.

"Where is he?" people ask. "He isn't real," others answer. It could be an argument at a dinner table this week. It's a line from a hymn in the Rig Veda, book two, and the god being doubted is Indra: the storm, the warrior, the one who breaks the dam and lets the rivers run. The hymn could have left the doubters out. Instead it quotes them, right in the middle of the praise. Today: the second voice, Indra.
screen: `"WHERE IS HE?"` → `"HE ISN'T REAL."` → `A HYMN THAT QUOTES ITS DOUBTERS.`

segments.voice: Indra is the mighty one of the Rig Veda's storms. In its stories he fights Vritra, a serpent coiled around the waters, and when Indra strikes him down, the rivers pour free. Book two, hymn twelve, praises him in a shape you can hear even in paraphrase. Verse after verse tells something he did: he steadied the shaking earth, spread out the sky, killed the serpent and set the rivers flowing. And verse after verse ends the same way. Sa janasa indrah. He, O people, is Indra. Then, in the fifth verse, the hymn turns. In paraphrase: the terrible one, about whom they ask, where is he? About whom they say, he is not. The singer's answer isn't an argument. It's shrad asmai dhatta: put your trust in him. Listen to those two phrases, because Hindu tradition still uses them. He is not has na asti in it: is not. The same two words later give Sanskrit its word nastika, one who says, there is not. And put your trust holds the roots of shraddha: faith, trust you choose to place, which many scholars hear as setting your heart on something. Here's the teaching. The Veda doesn't hide doubt. It names the doubter in his own words, and answers with shraddha, not proof. Centuries later the Gita says a person is made of their shraddha: as your trust is, so are you.
screen: `"HE, O PEOPLE, IS INDRA."` · `"WHERE IS HE?" "HE IS NOT."` · `NA ASTI → NASTIKA.` · `SHRAD DHATTA → SHRADDHA: TRUST YOU PLACE.`

segments.voice: Let one honest doubt be asked, about God, or whether any of this is true, without arguing it away. Then do what the hymn does: place your trust somewhere, even something small: a name of God you grew up with, the people who taught you, the breath coming back. If you pray, say that name once, slowly, and let the doubt sit beside it. If you don't, simply notice where your trust already rests.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Indra. In Rig Veda two, twelve, each verse ends, he, O people, is Indra; one verse quotes those who say, he is not, and answers, put your trust in him. Today's word.
Your line: shraddha, trust you place, even beside doubt. The hymn kept the doubter's words and still sang. Go gently.

howItsDone: Hymns to Indra are part of the Rig Veda's recitation, kept in Vedic schools; in later Hindu stories Indra appears as king of the gods and lord of rain.

chat.meaning: Rig Veda 2.12 quotes those who say of Indra, he is not, and answers: put your trust in him. The tradition names doubt out loud and answers it with shraddha, trust you choose to place.
